title: Count structural novelty separately from finish
when: Comparing alternatives or claiming breadth of exploration.
rule: Record material, typography, composition, information structure and behavior as separate dimensions. A new surface recipe is a valid exploration, but is not automatically a new design philosophy or interaction model.
counterexample: Calling sixteen glass treatments sixteen different navigation systems.
correction: The sixteen G studies use four recorded layout labels. Describe them as sixteen material explorations across four static layout families; behavior remains untested.
check: Compare the actual reading order, grouping and action placement before counting a structural difference.

title: Use material to establish hierarchy
when: Glass, texture, transparency or simulated physical surfaces surround decisions.
rule: Keep evidence and consequential actions on a stable reading plane. Use material to distinguish navigation or peripheral layers, with an explicit accessibility fallback in the implementation.
counterexample: A frosted file list looks legible on one wallpaper but loses label separation on another.
correction: Test changing backgrounds and system appearance settings; use a stable content surface where necessary. Static blur does not establish native Liquid Glass behavior.
check: Verify real text contrast, increased contrast, reduced transparency and focus appearance in the native prototype.

title: Separate measurement, estimate, scenario and target
when: Showing storage, savings, forecasts or reserve goals.
rule: Label current measured space, estimated candidates, conditional possible space, user target and remaining gap independently. Attach scope and measurement time when real data becomes available.
counterexample: The screen calls 98.5 GB available before the proposed 34.6 GB has been reviewed or removed.
correction: Show 63.9 GB current, 34.6 GB candidate estimate, 98.5 GB possible after review, and a 150 GB target. These study numbers are illustrative, not a scan.
check: Can a reader distinguish what exists now from what might happen, without relying on color?

title: Separate review, authorization, action and result
when: An interface can delete, uninstall, replace or otherwise change user data.
rule: A review entry point must open evidence. Show the exact selection and consequence before execution; report measured results only after the operation. A style never grants deletion authority.
counterexample: A button labeled Review immediately removes files, or a success illustration appears while the operation is still pending.
correction: Use distinct review, selection, execution and result states. Keep recovery or recreation limitations next to the relevant action.
check: Trace one file from discovery to review, explicit selection, operation and observed outcome, including a failure.

title: Do not let personality invent trust
when: Using friendly characters, industrial authority, warning palettes, rewards or ecological metaphors.
rule: Tone may orient and reassure through clarity. It must not imply that a file is safe, an action approved, a deadline urgent or a deletion environmentally beneficial without evidence.
counterexample: A smiling assistant, green leaf or official-looking console makes unknown files appear certified safe.
correction: Keep uncertainty and consequences explicit. Reserve urgency for an evidenced condition and avoid rewarding the amount deleted.
check: Can the same design communicate an unknown owner, failed uninstall and irreversible loss without softening their meaning?

title: Choose quantitative form by the comparison task
when: Encoding amounts, hierarchy, progress or change.
rule: Choose an encoding for the question being answered. Define units, scope, scale or denominator and provide exact values. Equal category tiles are categories, not proportional byte counts.
counterexample: A treemap omits its parent scope, or a waffle suggests that the 150 GB reserve target is the computer's disk capacity.
correction: Label the relevant whole and hierarchy. For exact category comparison, provide aligned numerical rows alongside the visual.
check: Ask a concrete question such as which candidate category is larger, or how much reserve remains; test accuracy and time before choosing an encoding.

title: Translate a reference into bounded design grammar
when: Borrowing from historical movements, cultural references or another platform.
rule: Name the specific borrowed feature and its limitation. A palette or motif is a translation study, not proof that a whole philosophy or cultural tradition has been understood or reproduced.
counterexample: A muted palette alone is labeled a complete philosophy, or nostalgia imports tiny controls and obsolete affordances.
correction: Describe the visible rhythm, type, edge, composition or material. Retain current readability and interaction semantics; identify where the reference stops.
check: Remove the title: can the claimed design grammar still be observed in the artifact?

title: Match navigation and disclosure to the task
when: Choosing lists, columns, accordions, inspectors, spatial canvases or command views.
rule: Use hierarchy to navigate paths, aligned lists to compare items, and disclosure for optional detail. Keep context and mandatory consequences available throughout the decision.
counterexample: Every file consequence is hidden in a collapsed accordion, forcing users to open all rows before a consequential action.
correction: Show shared mandatory facts in the review surface and use disclosure for supplementary detail. Preserve selection and the current path when switching views.
check: Complete the same file-review task with many items and a long path; measure extra navigation and missed evidence.

title: Prove accessibility on the implemented surface
when: Moving from static exploration to a working reader or native product.
rule: Static readability is only one check. Verify contrast, keyboard access, focus order, names and roles, resizing, long content and system preferences in the implementation.
counterexample: A screenshot with readable text is described as a fully accessible application.
correction: Report exactly what was checked and which interaction or assistive-technology checks remain. Supplement color with text or shape for meaning.
check: Use the real surface with keyboard, enlarged content and narrow width; inspect accessibility semantics and test assistive technology before release.

title: Prevent ornament from pretending to be data
when: Using repeated icons, rings, bars, silhouettes or spatial area near metrics.
rule: Any visual dimension that resembles a quantitative encoding needs either a defined mapping or a less ambiguous form. Decoration should not be mistaken for a count, amount or active control.
counterexample: Six icons appear under categories with different amounts, or a silo's arbitrary height looks like its storage usage.
correction: Use one categorical icon, remove arbitrary scale cues, or define and label a consistent data mapping. Keep the exact amount in text.
check: Ask what the number of marks, their height or ring length means before explaining it; redesign if interpretations conflict.

title: Keep claims within the available evidence
when: Writing rationales, safety labels, recommendations or learning claims.
rule: Check written intent against the rendered artifact and observed behavior. Preserve unknowns. Neither visual polish nor an estimate establishes implementation, approval, safety or effectiveness.
counterexample: X15 claims a KEEP/REVIEW/SPACE semantic map but renders a large slogan; X36 describes three switchable views but renders two static value panels.
correction: Mark these rationales for correction or implement and test the promised structure later. This foundation records author analysis, not user validation or model-weight training.
check: For each claim, identify an observable artifact, a verified behavior or an explicitly labeled hypothesis.
